newsitem.title: BURUNDI: Burundi political changes meet with scorn.
newsitem.headline: Burundi political changes meet with scorn.

text.p: Burundi's rebels and main Tutsi and Hutu parties dismissed the lifting of bans by military ruler Pierre Buyoya on Friday as a bid to loosen the grip of sanctions.
The Tutsi-dominated Burundian army meanwhile said its troops killed seven Hutu rebels on Thursday from a group that killed Burundi's senior Roman Catholic prelate in an ambush on Monday.
Buyoya's military-apppointed government announced late on Thursday it was immediately lifting bans on all political parties and the national assembly imposed since a July 25 coup.
Charles Mukasi, leader of the Tutsi-dominated Uprona party, responded by saying parliament had no real power even before Buyoya took over in the army coup and it would stay powerless.

"Lifting the ban on parliament is a cosmetic change simply designed to please (Julius) Nyerere," Mukasi told Reuters. The former Tanzanian president is the main mediator on Burundi and master-minded sanctions imposed by regional states on July 31.

"They are restoring an institution that was incapable of functioning. Power is held by the government," added Mukasi, a Hutu. He said he was pleased by the lifting of the ban on political parties because Uprona had been unfairly penalised.

If genuine, the changes meet two of the three conditions set by regional African leaders before they would remove the embargo on the landlocked country. The third condition is unconditional peace negotiations among all parties including Hutu rebels.
"This is a good step, but really it is not enough," said Jerome Ndiho, spokesman for the National Council for the Defence of Democracy (CNDD), political wing of the main rebel group.
"It cannot be effective until the security of the politicians can be guaranteed, and that can only happen when the army becomes truly national," Ndiho said in Brussels.
CNDD officials said the moves were an attempt by Buyoya to win an easing of sanctions but they should be maintained.
In Nairobi, a spokesman for exiled members of the Hutu-dominated Frodebu party said the changes did not amount to anything.

Joseph Ntakarutimana, a parliamentarian, said parliament would not be able to function while constitutional rule was not restored and most Frodebu deputies were forced to remain in exile because of attacks by the army and Tutsi militias.
But at the German ambassador's residence in Bujumbura where he took refuge during the coup, Leonce Ngendakumana, the Hutu president of the national assembly, welcomed the concessions.
"We will participate on condition it is the old national assembly and there are no named deputies," he told Reuters, adding he wanted to see talks between the government and rebels.
An army spokesman said on Friday 50 soldiers clashed on Thursday with rebels at Gitongo, where Archbishop Joachim Ruhuna and two nuns were killed when their car was ambushed on Monday.
"The rebels who attacked the soldiers are the same ones who killed the archbishop," said Lieutenant-Colonel Isaie Nibizi, adding there were no army casualties and the other rebels fled.
"We are still trying to secure the area around the car. We haven't started searching for the body (of Ruhana) yet," said Nibizi, showing how little control troops have in some regions.

Four people with the archbishop survived Monday's ambush in Gitega province. A Burundian nun killed in the attack was buried on Wednesday but the bodies of Ruhuna and another nun have not been recovered.
